summary: Marcus, a student, is confronted by a teacher, Mr. Wilson's counterpart (unnamed in this excerpt, referred to as 'he'), over a classroom outburst in the social studies class where the teacher had said the Constitution was not religious doctrine. Marcus defends his anger about the death of his friend Darryl and the loss of freedom after the bridge bombing, quotes the Declaration of Independence, refuses to apologize, and is suspended for two weeks under the school's zero-tolerance policy. At home he watches the TV news, which his parents rely on, and the news is full of fear about American soldiers dying abroad.
one_line: A student is suspended for two weeks after clashing with a social studies teacher over post-bombing politics and free government.
key_facts: Marcus is watched on a video feed from the social studies classroom while the teacher confronts him.
Marcus says the teacher's lesson 'wasn't teaching, it was propaganda' and that she told the class the Constitution didn't matter.
The teacher responds that she said the Constitution was not religious doctrine and that Marcus attacked her like a fundamentalist.
The teacher says everything changed when the bridge was bombed and mentions Marcus's friend Darryl.
Marcus tells the teacher not to say a word about Darryl and states that the country used to be free but now is not.
The teacher warns Marcus about 'zero-tolerance' policy, which can expel students for 'threatening behavior.'
Marcus decides he would rather get kicked out than apologize to the teacher.
Marcus recites the Declaration of Independence passage beginning 'Governments are instituted among men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed.'
The teacher replies, 'Remembering things isn't the same as understanding them, sonny.'
Marcus is handed a sheet of Board letterhead saying he has been suspended for two weeks.
The teacher says he will email Marcus's parents and that Marcus will be arrested for trespassing if still on school property after thirty minutes.
Marcus throws the letter on the kitchen table when he gets home and then watches the TV, which his parents watch for their ideas about the world.
The news Marcus sees says American soldiers are dying all over the world, including National Guardsmen.
